O6.name: Nara
O6.why: Japan's first permanent capital: Great Buddha, forest shrine, old merchant quarter; on the way from Yoshino to Osaka.
O6.access: Kintetsu-Nara Stn; everything is on foot (the loop is ~5 km).
see: O6f Naramachi and lunch.
O6a Kōfuku-ji.
O6g Yoshikien.
O6b Nara Park and the deer.
O6c Tōdai-ji.
O6d Kasuga Taisha.
O6e Nigatsu-dō sunset.

route.enter: Kintetsu-Nara Stn, exit 2, south to Naramachi.
walk: Naramachi → Kōfuku-ji → Yoshikien → Tōdai-ji → Kasuga Taisha → Nigatsu-dō.
route.exit: Nigatsu-dō → Kintetsu-Nara ~20–25 min on foot, 17:47 train to Osaka-Namba.

facts: Heijō-kyō (Nara) was the capital from 710 to 784.
The temples and shrines form the UNESCO site 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara' (1998).
tips: Keep paper and maps out of the deer's reach; they eat them.

O6a.name: Kōfuku-ji
O6a.desc: Fujiwara family temple; the Ashura statue (pagoda hidden by repairs)
O6a.why: Old statues and golden halls, 10 min from Naramachi. ⚠️ The five-storey pagoda is fully covered for repairs (until ~2031) and can't be seen.
O6a.hours: Grounds 24 h. Halls and National Treasure Museum 9:00–17:00 (last entry 16:45).
O6a.price: Grounds free. Central Golden Hall ¥500, Eastern Golden Hall ¥500, National Treasure Museum ¥900; all three ¥1,600.
O6a.stay: 30 min (grounds) or 45–60 min with the museum
O6a.access: 5 min from Kintetsu-Nara; 10 min north of Naramachi via Sarusawa Pond.
see: National Treasure Museum: the three-faced, six-armed Ashura (734).
Central Golden Hall, rebuilt in 2018 for the first time in 300 years.
Eastern Golden Hall (Tōkondō).
Sarusawa Pond below the temple.
Northern Octagonal Hall (outside).

route.enter: From Sarusawa Pond up the 52 steps (Gojūni-dan).
walk: Central Golden Hall → (museum) → Eastern Golden Hall → covered pagoda site → Northern Octagonal Hall.
route.exit: North-east across Noborioji-dōri to Yoshikien (~7 min).

facts: Family temple of the Fujiwara, the clan that ran the imperial court for centuries; moved to Nara in 710.
The pagoda (1426, ~50 m) is Japan's second-tallest wooden pagoda after Tō-ji's in Kyoto.
tips: If time is short, pick the museum (Ashura) over the halls.

O6b.name: Nara Park
O6b.why: Walk-through between the sights; the deer are pushiest 10:00–15:00.
O6b.access: Between Kōfuku-ji, Tōdai-ji and Kasuga Taisha.
see: The deer bowing for crackers.
Ukimidō, the pavilion on Sagi-ike pond (south side, if passing).
facts: The deer are protected as a National Natural Monument; about 1,700 were counted in 2026.
Legend: Kasuga's god arrived on a white deer, so deer became sacred messengers.
tips: Feed only shika senbei, show empty hands when done, and watch for head-butts and bites.
Don't feed them human food or plastic.

O6c.name: Tōdai-ji
O6c.why: Nearly 15 m bronze Buddha in a huge wooden hall.
O6c.hours: Daibutsuden Nov–Mar 8:00–17:00. Hokke-dō and Kaidan-dō 8:30–16:00. Museum 9:30–17:00.
O6c.access: ~10 min north of Yoshikien through the park.
see: Nandaimon gate and its two 8.4 m Niō guardians (1203, by Unkei and Kaikei).
Daibutsu (Vairocana Buddha), ~15 m.
The pillar with a hole the size of the Buddha's nostril.
Binzuru statue by the exit: rub the part of him that matches where you hurt.

walk: Clockwise inside the hall: Buddha, side bodhisattvas, guardian kings, the pillar.
route.exit: East exit, then up the stone lane towards Nigatsu-dō or south-east to Kasuga Taisha.

facts: The Buddha was dedicated in 752; the head and hands are later recasts after fires.
The hall was rebuilt in 1709 at about two-thirds of its original width and is still one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.
tips: 📿 stamp.

O6d.name: Kasuga Taisha
O6d.why: Forest paths and thousands of lanterns.
O6d.price: Grounds free. Special worship ¥700 (the English official page still says ¥500).
O6d.access: ~15 min south-east of Tōdai-ji along the lantern path; bus stop Kasuga Taisha Honden.
see: Path of about 2,000 stone lanterns from the first torii.
Vermilion main sanctuary inside the corridor (special worship).
Fujinami-no-ya: a dark hall lit by hanging bronze lanterns.
Kasugayama Primeval Forest along the path.

route.enter: First torii (Ichi-no-torii) on the west side of the park, then the lantern path; or from Tōdai-ji via the Wakakusa side.
walk: Main hall area → special worship → Fujinami-no-ya → back out.
route.exit: North path ~15 min uphill to Nigatsu-dō (past Wakakusa-yama base).

facts: Founded in 768 by the Fujiwara to protect the new capital.
About 3,000 lanterns in total (stone and bronze), donated over 1,000 years; all are lit only at the Mantōrō festivals in February and August.
tips: Enter the special worship before 16:00.
📿 stamp.

O6e.name: Nigatsu-dō
O6e.desc: Wooden balcony over Nara at sunset
O6e.why: Free sunset view over the Great Buddha Hall roof; sunset ~16:50.
O6e.access: Up the stone steps east of the Daibutsuden (~10 min), part of Tōdai-ji.
see: Balcony view west over the Daibutsuden roof to the Ikoma hills.
Covered stone stairway on the north side.
Hokke-dō (Sangatsu-dō) next door, Tōdai-ji's oldest building (closes 16:00).

route.enter: Covered stairs on the north side.
route.exit: Down through the Tōdai-ji lanes, west to Kintetsu-Nara (~20–25 min).

facts: Shuni-e (Omizutori), with giant torches on this balcony, has been held every March since 752 without a single year missed.
The present hall was rebuilt in 1669 after a fire during the ceremony.
tips: Dark paths after sunset: phone torch.

O6f.name: Naramachi
O6f.why: Old streets and kakinoha-zushi (persimmon-leaf sushi) for lunch.
see: Narrow machiya houses with lattice fronts.
Red migawari-zaru (substitute monkey) charms hanging under eaves.
Gangō-ji (World Heritage, roof tiles from the 6th century) at the centre, outside view.
Kōshin-dō, the small hall of the monkey charms.

route.enter: From Sarusawa Pond south along Mochiidono shopping street.
walk: Gangō-ji → Kōshin-dō → lunch → north back to the pond.

facts: Naramachi grew in the Edo period on land that once belonged to Gangō-ji, one of Japan's oldest temples.
tips: Kakinoha-zushi keeps well: buy some for the evening train.

O6g.name: Yoshikien Garden
O6g.why: Garden between Kōfuku-ji and Tōdai-ji, autumn colours, few visitors.
O6g.hours: 9:00–17:00, last entry 16:30. Closed only in late February.
O6g.access: ~7 min from Kōfuku-ji; next to Isuien (paid, skipped).
see: Pond garden.
Moss garden with a thatched tea house.
Tea-flower garden.

route.enter: Main gate on the lane by the Yoshiki River.
walk: Pond → moss garden → tea garden (one loop).
route.exit: Same gate; north through the park to Tōdai-ji (~10 min).

facts: Built in 1919 on the site of a Kōfuku-ji sub-temple; the prefecture opened it to the public in 1989.
tips: Bring passports for free entry.

O23.name: Nara National Museum
O23.why: Japan's best Buddhist statue collection, in the park between Tōdai-ji and Kasuga Taisha; rain backup, no detour.
O23.hours: 9:30–17:00, last entry 16:30; closed Mon (open Thu 19). Shōsōin exhibition ended 9 Nov.
see: Nara Buddhist Sculpture Hall: about 100 statues from the 600s to the 1300s.
Ancient Chinese bronzes hall (underground corridor).
facts: The sculpture hall (1894) by Katayama Tōkuma was Nara's first Western-style building.
tips: Pick up the English brochure on the statues at the entrance.

O24.name: Mt. Wakakusa
O24.why: Open grass hill with a wide view over Nara and deer on the slopes; instead of Nigatsu-dō, not both.
O24.hours: 9:00–17:00; open until the 2nd Sunday of December.
see: First viewpoint (~15 min up): the city and the Daibutsuden roof.
Summit (342 m), ~30 min.
facts: Every January the whole hillside is set on fire after fireworks (Yamayaki).
tips: Gates close 17:00 and sunset is ~16:50: be on your way down by then.

O1.name: Osaka Castle
O1.desc: 1620s Tokugawa walls and moats; where Adams met Ieyasu
O1.why: Where William Adams met Ieyasu in 1600; the walls and moats are the original Tokugawa rebuild.
O1.hours: Park 24 h, free. Keep 9:00–18:00 (last entry 17:30). Autumn turret openings are weekends only.
O1.price: Grounds free. Keep ¥1,200 (includes the Toyotomi Stone Wall Museum, opened 2025). Keep skipped (decided).
O1.access: Osakajōkōen Stn (JR Loop Line) for the tour meeting point; Tanimachi 4-chōme for Nishinomaru Garden.
O1.booking: BOOKED: Ghosts of Osaka Castle tour, Sat 21 17:00–19:00, grounds only, ref GYGBLG88YW8R.
see: Ōte-mon gate (1628) and its huge stone blocks.
Tako-ishi ('octopus stone') inside Sakura-mon: the largest stone in the walls, about 130 tonnes.
Daimyō crests carved on the wall stones.
The keep from the Honmaru plaza (outside).
Inner and outer moats; the 30 m walls of the Honmaru on the east side.
Optional: Toyotomi Stone Wall Museum, showing Hideyoshi's original buried wall (needs the keep ticket).

route.enter: Nishinomaru Garden side at ~15:45, then walk past the walls to the meeting point at the Starbucks on Jo Terrace, in front of Osaka-Jo Hall (by 16:50).
walk: The Ghosts of Osaka Castle tour route, 17:00–19:00, grounds only.
route.exit: Ends at the meeting point, right outside JR Osakajōkōen Stn.

facts: Hideyoshi built the first castle from 1583; it was destroyed in the 1615 siege that ended the Toyotomi line.
The Tokugawa rebuilt it from 1620 to 1629 on top of the old castle; about 60 daimyō each built a section of wall.
The keep is a 1931 concrete reconstruction, paid for by public donations from Osaka citizens.
tips: Gojōin card at the keep shop, not a 📿 stamp.
Morinomiya side has konbini and cafés for lunch.

O1a.name: Nishinomaru Garden
O1a.why: Lawn garden below the keep with the best view of it; optional after the guide.
O1a.access: West side of the castle, inside the Ōte-mon area.
see: The keep across the moat, framed by trees.
Hōshō-an teahouse in the north-east corner (outside view).
facts: The site was the residence of Nene, Hideyoshi's wife, before she moved to Kyoto (Kōdai-ji, K1e).
The Hōshō-an teahouse was donated in 1969 by Matsushita Kōnosuke, founder of Panasonic.

O2.name: Noda Central Market, Endo Sushi
O2.why: Sushi breakfast inside a working wholesale market; dropped for a lighter Friday (Kizu instead).
O2.hours: Endo 5:00–14:00 Mon–Sat; market closed Sun, holidays and some Wed (not re-checked: not included).
see: Five pieces of sushi per plate, the classic order.
facts: Endo has served market workers since 1931.

O3.name: Tenjinbashi-suji
O3.desc: Longest shopping street in Japan, local snacks
O3.why: 2.6 km of everyday Osaka shops and snacks, almost no tourists.
O3.access: South end at Osaka Tenmangū (Minami-morimachi / Ōsaka-Temmangū Stn); north end at Tenjinbashisuji 6-chōme Stn.
see: Osaka Tenmangū shrine at the 1-chōme end.
Croquette and fried-snack stands.
Old kissaten coffee shops, sweet shops, cheap clothing and household shops.
Ōsaka Kurashi no Konjakukan (housing museum) near 6-chōme, if time (closed Tue).

walk: North through 1- to 6-chōme; side lanes have small bars and izakaya.
route.exit: Around 4–5-chōme, cut west to Nakazakichō (O11) or continue to 6-chōme Stn.

facts: About 600 shops; the arcade grew from the market street to Osaka Tenmangū, founded in 949 for the scholar Sugawara no Michizane.
tips: Snack as you go, but eat standing at the stall.

O4.name: Shinsekai kushikatsu
O4.why: Retro 1910s district, home of kushikatsu, two stops from our stay.
O4.hours: Most kushikatsu shops ~11:00–22:30; many open late.
O4.access: Dōbutsuen-mae Stn (Midōsuji / Sakaisuji Line) or Ebisuchō Stn; ~10 min from Tamade.
see: Tsūtenkaku tower (1956, 103 m) and the lucky god Billiken.
Jan-Jan Yokochō, the narrow covered alley of cheap eateries and shōgi parlours.
Neon puffer-fish and dragon signs.

walk: Up to Tsūtenkaku; choose a kushikatsu shop in the side streets (Daruma is the famous chain; smaller local ones are quieter).
route.exit: Ebisuchō or Dōbutsuen-mae; Daikokuchō → Tamade ~7 min.

facts: Shinsekai ('New World') opened in 1912, its north half modelled on Paris and its south half on New York's Coney Island.
Kushikatsu became the area's food in the 1920s: cheap fried skewers for labourers.
tips: Never dip a bitten skewer into the shared sauce; use the cabbage to scoop sauce.
Rough at night in places but safe; keep to the main streets.

O5.name: Kobe beef dinner
O5.desc: Certified restaurant; O5a or O5e, decided on the fly
O5.why: The trip's splurge dinner; Kobe itself was dropped.
O5.booking: Not booked; book the same day or the day before.
see: Ask for the cut's certificate number; certified shops show a bronze nojigiku (wild chrysanthemum) statue and a membership plaque.
facts: Only Tajima-breed cattle born and raised in Hyōgo that pass strict grading can be sold as Kobe beef; each animal has a 10-digit ID you can look up.
The brand association was set up in 1983.
tips: Check the shop at kobe-niku.jp/shop before going.
O5.pending: Choose O5e (Fri 20 lunch or evening) or O5a (Sat 21) on the fly.
O5.decision: P1; lunch or dinner, decide later

O5a.name: Techangum Shinsaibashi Honten
O5a.why: Yakiniku with certified Kobe beef, ~¥13,000 pp; 10–15 min walk from Dōtonbori.
O5a.booking: Gurunavi online, free and instant (gurunavi.com/ja/ka42605/rst), or tel. 06-6121-8803.
see: Kobe beef cuts grilled yourself at the table.
facts: Yakiniku (Korean-style table grilling) took off in Osaka after WWII.
tips: ⚠️ The Gurunavi listing marks it as smoking allowed: ask for non-smoking when booking.
Confirm the Kobe beef certificate on the menu.
O5a.decision: Option for Sat 21 ~20:15, decide on the fly

O5e.name: Kobe Steak Ishida LINKS Umeda
O5e.why: Chef-grilled Kobe beef at the counter, 1 min from JR Osaka, right after Umeda Sky.
O5e.price: Dinner courses from ¥6,380 (A5 wagyu); Kobe beef courses higher (~¥13,000+).
O5e.access: LINKS UMEDA 8F, Ōfukachō, Kita-ku; JR Osaka Stn 1 min.
O5e.booking: Gurunavi online (gurunavi.com/ja/c192812/rst), or My Concierge Japan (prepayment, +10% fee). Tel. 06-6147-8325.
see: Teppanyaki: the chef cooks in front of you.
facts: Ishida is a Kobe-based group; a Kansai Walker article says the shop serves Kobe beef with its 'Kobe-no-niku' certificate.
tips: Courses with 'A5 黒毛和牛' are wagyu, not Kobe beef: choose a course labelled 神戸牛 / Kobe beef.
O5e.decision: Option 3, Fri 20 lunch; or Fri 20 evening

O7.name: Hankai tram + Sumiyoshi Taisha
O7.desc: Osaka's last streetcar to one of Japan's oldest shrines
O7.why: Osaka's last streetcar line to the head shrine of 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines.
O7.hours: Oct–Mar 6:30–17:00 (outer gate 16:00); shrine office for stamps ~9:00–17:00.
O7.access: Hankai Uemachi Line Tennōji-ekimae → Sumiyoshi-toriimae (~20 min); stop at the gate. Back: Nankai Sumiyoshitaisha Stn, 3 min.
see: Sori-hashi, the steep red arched bridge.
Four main halls in Sumiyoshi-zukuri style (National Treasures, rebuilt 1810).
Gosho-gozen: a fenced gravel plot where people search for stones marked 五, 大 and 力.
Over 600 stone lanterns donated by merchants and shipowners.

route.enter: Main torii by the tram stop → Sori-hashi.
walk: First to fourth halls → Gosho-gozen (behind the first hall area) → sub-shrines.
route.exit: West to Nankai Sumiyoshitaisha Stn (3 min).

facts: Traditionally founded in 211; its building style predates Buddhist influence on shrine architecture.
The gods are sea deities who protect sailors and diplomats.
tips: Tram: pay ¥230 when you get off (IC cards work).
📿 stamp.

O8.name: Umeda Sky Building
O8.why: Open-air rooftop ring 173 m over Osaka, on the route.
O8.access: ~7–10 min walk north-west of JR Osaka, through an underpass (follow the signs).
see: The glass-tube escalator from 35F to 39F, crossing between the towers.
The open-air Floating Garden on the roof (40F+).
Glowing floor and night view over the Yodo River.

route.enter: East tower lift to 35F, then the escalator to 39F (ticket desk).
walk: 39F indoor deck → stairs/escalator to the rooftop ring.
route.exit: Same way; Umeda Stn (Midōsuji Line) ~10 min.

facts: Opened in 1993; architect Hara Hiroshi. The top floors were built on the ground and lifted into place between the towers.
tips: Windy and cold on the roof in November: jacket.
Sunset ~16:50; at 18:15 it's the night view.

O9.name: Hōzen-ji Yokochō
O9.desc: Stone lantern alley, moss-covered Fudō statue
O9.why: A slice of old Osaka right behind Dōtonbori.
O9.access: Between Dōtonbori and Sennichimae, ~5 min from Namba Stn.
see: Mizukake Fudō: the statue completely green with moss from centuries of splashed water.
The two flagstone alleys (80 m) with lanterns and old restaurants.
Meoto Zenzai (1883): sweet red-bean soup served in two small bowls for couples.
facts: The temple was founded in 1637; the 1945 air raids destroyed everything except the Fudō statue.
tips: Ladle water onto the statue and make a wish; it's how the moss grew.

O10.name: Shitennō-ji
O10.desc: Temple founded 593; flea market on the 21st
O10.why: One of Japan's oldest temples, and on Sat 21 its big monthly flea market.
O10.hours: Outer grounds 24 h. Central precinct and garden Oct–Mar 8:30–16:00; on the 21st 8:00–16:30. Last entry 30 min before closing.
O10.price: Outer grounds free. Central precinct ¥300–500 (sources differ); garden ¥300; Treasure House ¥500.
O10.access: Shitennoji-mae Yūhigaoka Stn (Tanimachi Line), ~5 min; Tamade ~22 min, ¥240.
see: Daishi-e flea market (~500 stalls): antiques, kimono, tools, food; best before 10:00.
Central precinct: Chūmon gate, five-storey pagoda, Kondō and Kōdō in one straight line.
Gokuraku-jōdo garden (pond, stone bridges).
Ishi-no-torii (1294), one of the oldest stone torii in Japan.

route.enter: Nishi-mon (west gate) and the stone torii.
walk: Flea market in the outer grounds first (before 10:00) → central precinct → garden.
route.exit: Back to Shitennoji-mae Yūhigaoka, or walk ~12 min south to Tennōji for the tram.

facts: Founded in 593 by Prince Shōtoku as Japan's first state-built Buddhist temple.
The present buildings are mostly a 1963 concrete reconstruction of the original layout.
tips: Cash for the market.
Goshuin not verified.

O11.name: Nakazakichō
O11.why: Quiet pre-war lanes next to busy Umeda.
O11.hours: Streets 24 h; cafés ~11:00–18:00/19:00 (vary, many close early or on Tue/Wed).
O11.access: Nakazakichō Stn (Tanimachi Line), exit 2; ~10 min walk from Umeda.
see: Nagaya (row houses) with tiled roofs and tiny gardens.
Ivy-covered cafés, zakka shops and galleries.
facts: The area escaped the 1945 firebombing, so it kept its pre-war houses next to Umeda's towers.
tips: Residential: quiet voices, no photos of people's homes.
O11.decision: Fri 20, by option, or Sun 22 morning

O12.name: Kuromon Market
O12.why: Quick look only; touristy and overpriced.
O12.access: Nippombashi Stn, ~5 min; ~10 min walk from Nankai Namba.
see: 580 m covered arcade, ~150 shops: fugu, crab, scallops, wagyu skewers, fruit.
facts: The name ('black gate') comes from the black gate of Enmyō-ji temple, which once stood nearby.
tips: Prices are high; compare with Kizu (O15).

O13.name: Dōtonbori
O13.why: The neon canal at night; walk, don't eat there.
see: Glico running-man sign from Ebisu bridge.
Kani Dōraku's moving crab and Kuidaore Tarō the drummer clown.
Tombori river walk along the canal (quieter, below street level).
facts: The canal was dug from 1612 by the merchant Yasui Dōton, who died fighting for the Toyotomi in the 1615 siege; his cousin finished it and named it after him.
tips: Pickpocket-aware in crowds.

O14.name: Hosokawa Gracia statue
O14.desc: Shōgun's Mariko, at Osaka Cathedral on the Hosokawa mansion site
O14.why: A real Shōgun site near the castle, 20–30 min.
O14.hours: Outdoor statues 24 h; cathedral usually open in the daytime.
O14.access: ~15 min walk from the castle's Tamatsukuri side; Tamatsukuri Stn 10 min.
see: Statues of Hosokawa Gracia and the Christian daimyō Takayama Ukon in front of St Mary's Cathedral.
Inside: large paintings of Gracia (if open).
facts: Gracia (Tama, 1563–1600) was a daughter of Akechi Mitsuhide and a Christian convert.
In 1600 she refused to become Ishida Mitsunari's hostage; as a Christian she could not take her own life, so her retainer killed her and burned the mansion.
tips: Quiet: it's a working church.

O15.name: Kizu Market
O15.why: Local market breakfast 3 metro stops from our stay, much cheaper and calmer than Kuromon.
O15.hours: Shops ~6:00–11:00 (eateries from ~5:00, some to 13:00). Closed Sun, holidays and some Wed.
O15.access: Daikokuchō Stn exit 1, 3 min; Tamade → Daikokuchō 3 stops (Yotsubashi Line).
see: Kizu Uoichi Shokudō: seafood bowls (opens 6:00, closes when sold out).
Fish, produce and pickle stalls for chefs.
Shokuzai Center ODA supermarket.
facts: The market dates from around 1710 and is one of Japan's largest privately run wholesale markets.
tips: Cash only.
Shops close towards 11:00: be there by 9:00.
O15.decision: Your pick; morning, near the stay

O16.name: Usami-tei Matsubaya
O16.why: Lets you check a fact from your trivia list; cheap and quick.
see: Kitsune udon (sweet fried tofu on udon).
Ojiya udon: udon with rice and egg in an iron pot.
facts: Listed in Tabelog's 'Udon 100 West' 2024.
tips: Queue at lunchtime; go before 12:00 or after 13:30.

O17.name: Yoshino Sushi
O17.desc: Inventor of hako-zushi pressed sushi, since 1841
O17.why: Great history, but closed Sat, Sun and holidays, so only Fri 20 lunch is possible.
O17.hours: Dine-in lunch 11:00–15:00 (L.O. 14:30); dinner 17:00–22:00 by reservation; closed Sat, Sun, holidays.
see: Hako-zushi: sea bream, conger eel, egg and prawn pressed in a box, cut in squares.
facts: Its hako-zushi is nicknamed 'kaiseki in 2 sun 6 bu', after the size of the box (about 8 cm square).
tips: Takeaway boxes travel well.

O18.name: Takoyaki and okonomiyaki
O18.why: Only a meal, no extra time needed.
see: Takoyaki: octopus in batter balls, turned with picks.
Okonomiyaki: cabbage pancake cooked on the table griddle.
facts: Takoyaki was created in Osaka in 1935 by Endō Tomekichi of Aizuya.
tips: Takoyaki are lava-hot inside: bite a hole first.

O19.name: Genpin Hōzen-ji Sōhonten
O19.desc: Torafugu course: sashimi, skin, hot pot, zōsui
O19.why: Fugu in Osaka, the classic fugu city, in season in November, next to Hōzen-ji Yokochō.
O19.hours: Weekdays 12:00–22:30, Sat, Sun and holidays 11:30–22:30; lunch menu L.O. 15:00.
O19.price: Autumn course 5 dishes ¥5,500 (Sep–Oct); November courses not yet listed.
O19.access: Namba 1-1-13, by Hōzen-ji; Namba Stn 2 min.
O19.booking: Ikyu online or tel. 06-6213-9444 (book by Wed 18).
see: Tessa (thin fugu sashimi), skin, tecchiri hot pot, then zōsui rice soup in the broth.
facts: Fugu chefs need a special licence; the poisonous parts are removed and locked away.
tips: Non-smoking; cards and PayPay accepted.

O20.name: 551 Hōrai
O20.desc: Pork buns since 1945; Namba main shop, Ebisubashi
O20.why: Osaka's favourite butaman: cheap, freshly steamed, a local institution.
O20.hours: Main shop restaurant 11:00–22:00 (L.O. 21:30); closed 1st and 3rd Tue (open Sat 21). Shin-Osaka Stn shop 9:00–21:30 daily.
see: Staff folding buns by hand behind the window.
facts: Founded in 1945; the main shop sells about 170,000 buns a day across the chain, all hand-folded.
tips: Strong smell: eat before boarding the Shinkansen or keep the box closed.

O21.name: Pathfinder XNOBU
O21.desc: Specialty coffee; Tenmangu takeaway stand / LUCUA café
O21.why: Your pick: specialty coffee right on the Day 10 route, no detour.
O21.hours: Tenmangu stand: hours not found (old note 10:00–18:00, verify). LUCUA 1100 4F: 10:30–20:00.
O21.access: Tenjinbashi 2-5-9, behind Osaka Tenmangū (start of Tenjinbashi-suji).
see: Melbourne-style flat whites and the 'rainbow latte'.
facts: The menu is supervised by a barista who trained in Melbourne and twice won a world latte-art title.
tips: Tenmangu stand is takeaway only.

O22.name: Katsuō-ji, Minoh
O22.why: Daruma-filled mountain temple at peak foliage, but a half day away; dropped.
see: Thousands of small red daruma on every ledge.
